entries.question: How are people judged by God?
entries.summary: The New Testament offers two incompatible criteria for divine judgment. Matthew 12:37, Luke 10:26-28, and John 5:29 anchor judgment in works — words, deeds, and obedience to the Torah's love command. Mark 16:16, John 3:3, John 3:18, and John 3:36 anchor it in belief — faith in the Son, or the new birth. The verses don't describe two facets of one rubric; they describe two different rubrics that determine eternal fate.
entries.commentary:
This is the classic faith-versus-works tension that has fractured Christian theology since the Reformation, and it's right there in the text before any later council weighs in. Matthew 12:37 puts it bluntly — "by thy words thou shalt be justified" — and John 5:29 doubles down on the deed criterion at the eschatological resurrection. Luke 10:26-28 has Jesus tell the lawyer that doing the Torah's love commands is the path to eternal life. Then Mark 16:16 and the Johannine pickup at 3:3, 3:18, and 3:36 swing the other way: belief saves, unbelief damns, and the only "work" that matters is being born again.

The standard harmonization runs through James 2:17 — faith without works is dead — and argues that real belief always produces deeds, so the two criteria collapse into one. Craig Blomberg makes this move, and so does the older Reformed reading that calls works the evidence of saving faith rather than its cause. The problem is that the Synoptic and Johannine passages aren't describing "evidence of belief." Luke 10:28 has Jesus tell the lawyer "this do, and thou shalt live" with no belief-clause attached. John 3:18 has people "condemned already" purely because they don't believe, with deeds not mentioned at all. The criteria are presented as sufficient on their own terms in their own passages.

More tellingly, the Mark 16:16 passage sits inside the Longer Ending — verses 9-20 — which the earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus, Vaticanus) don't contain. Metzger flags it as a near-certain later addition. So one of the strongest "belief alone" prooftexts probably wasn't in Mark's original gospel at all. The tension between deed-based judgment (Matthew, Luke, parts of John) and belief-based judgment (the Johannine farewell discourse, secondary Mark) reflects competing soteriological streams inside early Christianity that the canon never fully reconciled. Take your pick — the text doesn't pick for you.

entries.question: Does righteousness come from following the Law?
entries.summary: Luke 1:6 calls Zacharias and Elisabeth righteous specifically because they walked in all the Lord's commandments blameless, and Romans 2:13 states that doers of the Law shall be justified. Galatians 2:21 reverses course — if righteousness comes by the Law, Christ died for nothing. The Lukan and early-Pauline framing makes Torah-keeping a path to righteousness; the mature Paul forecloses that path entirely.
entries.commentary:
This one is a fault line that runs straight through Paul's own corpus. Romans 2:13 lays down the principle plainly: "the doers of the law shall be justified." In context Paul is arguing that God judges impartially, and the same standard applies to Jew and Gentile. Luke 1:6 then describes Zacharias and Elisabeth as "righteous before God walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blameless" — Lukan piety in continuity with Second Temple Jewish ideals. Galatians 2:21 burns the bridge: if righteousness could come through Law, Christ died for nothing.

The standard apologetic harmonization, championed by Douglas Moo and the Reformed tradition, says Romans 2:13 is hypothetical — Paul is describing a standard nobody actually meets, only to set up his "all have sinned" argument in Romans 3:23. So the Law could justify in principle, just not in practice. That's a defensible reading, but it doesn't dissolve the contradiction with Luke 1:6, which presents two real people as actually achieving blameless Law-observance. Luke doesn't say "they would have been righteous if anyone could keep the Law" — he says they did.

The deeper issue is that Paul himself moves. E. P. Sanders and the New Perspective on Paul scholars — James Dunn, N. T. Wright — argue that Paul's break with Torah-righteousness was a Christological inference, not a critique of Jewish legalism. Paul's logic in Galatians 2:21 is essentially: if Torah-keeping worked, the cross was unnecessary; the cross was necessary; therefore Torah-keeping doesn't work. That's a post-hoc rationalization driven by his commitment to the cross, not a derivation from prior premises about human capacity. Luke, writing later and from a different theological stream, doesn't share that commitment — he's comfortable with pious Jews being righteous by Torah-observance. The canon contains both streams without integrating them.

entries.question: Who was Jesus' grandfather on his father's side?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:16 names Joseph's father as Jacob, son of Matthan, in a Davidic line running through Solomon. Luke 3:23-24 names Joseph's father as Heli, son of Matthat, in a Davidic line running through Nathan. Both genealogies claim to trace Jesus' paternal lineage, and they disagree on the most basic fact — his grandfather's name — along with most of the names between David and Joseph.
entries.commentary:
Two genealogies, two grandfathers, and roughly forty different names in between. The discrepancy isn't a marginal textual variant — it's a structural problem. Matthew runs David to Joseph through Solomon and the royal line; Luke runs David to Joseph through Nathan, a different son. The names diverge almost completely. Matthan begets Jacob begets Joseph in Matthew. Matthat begets Heli begets Joseph in Luke. Same Joseph, two different fathers.

The classic harmonization, going back to Julius Africanus in the third century and revived by every generation of apologists since, is that one genealogy is Mary's. Gleason Archer pushes this hard: Luke is really tracing Mary's line through her father Heli, with Joseph listed only because Luke wanted a male name at the top. The problem is that Luke 3:23 explicitly says Jesus was "as was supposed" the son of Joseph, then names Heli as Joseph's father — not Mary's. The Greek doesn't support a Marian reading; the text says what it says.

The second harmonization is levirate marriage: Joseph's biological father was one man, his legal father another, because of a Deuteronomy 25:5-10 levirate arrangement. Eusebius preserves Africanus's version of this. The problem is that levirate marriage requires the deceased brother and the surviving brother to share a father, so the lines should converge somewhere — but Matthew and Luke don't converge at all between David and Joseph. You'd need a stacked sequence of levirate marriages across forty generations, which is the textbook definition of an ad-hoc rationalization.

The critical scholarly consensus, articulated by Raymond Brown in The Birth of the Messiah, is that the two genealogies are independent theological constructions. Matthew's Davidic-royal line establishes Jesus as the legitimate son of David through Solomon's throne. Luke's line, going back through Adam to God, establishes Jesus as a universal figure. Neither author had access to historical genealogical records covering a thousand years of Joseph's ancestry — that data didn't exist. They built genealogies that served their theological purposes, and they don't fit together.

entries.question: How many generations were there from David to Jesus?
entries.summary: Matthew 1:17 explicitly structures the genealogy in three groups of fourteen, yielding 27 generations from David to Jesus. Luke 3:23-31 lists 42 names from David to Jesus. The two evangelists count the same span of history and arrive at radically different numbers because they're tracing different lines.
entries.commentary:
This is a downstream consequence of the previous contradiction. Matthew runs David to Jesus through Solomon and the kings of Judah, structured numerically into three sets of fourteen — Matthew 1:17 spells it out. Luke runs David to Jesus through Nathan, a non-royal son, and the line is biologically longer by fifteen generations. Same starting point, same endpoint, two different counts.

The Matthean fourteen-fourteen-fourteen scheme is itself a theological construction. Davies and Allison point out in the ICC that Matthew has to drop three kings — Ahaziah, Joash, and Amaziah — from the Old Testament record to get his second set down to fourteen, and he counts Jeconiah twice to make the third set work. That's not a neutral historical list; it's a numerologically engineered structure, almost certainly built on the gematria of David's name in Hebrew (D-V-D = 4+6+4 = 14). Brown lays this out in The Birth of the Messiah.

The apologetic response is that ancient genealogies often skipped generations for stylistic reasons, so a 27-name list and a 42-name list can both be accurate at different levels of compression. That's true as a general principle — Old Testament genealogies do telescope — but it doesn't solve the problem here because Matthew and Luke aren't compressed versions of the same list. They have almost entirely different names. Compression preserves names while skipping others; these are two separate genealogical traditions.

The simpler explanation: neither evangelist had access to a thousand-year genealogical record for a Galilean carpenter's family, because such records didn't exist. Both built genealogies that served their respective theological agendas — Matthew the royal-Davidic schema, Luke the universal-Adamic schema — and they don't match because they were never working from the same source.

entries.question: Who washed Jesus's feet with her tears and dried his feet with her hair?
entries.summary: John 12:1-3 names Mary, the sister of Martha and Lazarus, anointing Jesus' feet at Bethany six days before Passover. Luke 7:36-38 places an unnamed sinful woman washing Jesus' feet with her tears at a Pharisee's house earlier in the ministry. Both narratives describe the same striking detail — a woman wiping Jesus' feet with her hair — but identify different women in different settings, and a long interpretive tradition further conflated both with Mary Magdalene.
entries.commentary:
There are four anointing stories in the gospels — Mark 14:3-9, Matthew 26:6-13, Luke 7:36-50, and John 12:1-8 — and the question is whether they describe one event, two events, or some messy combination. Mark and Matthew agree: anointing at Bethany, two days before Passover, in the house of Simon the Leper, an unnamed woman pouring ointment on Jesus' head. John 12 also puts it at Bethany but six days before Passover, in Lazarus's house, with Mary anointing Jesus' feet. Luke 7 puts it in Galilee, much earlier in the ministry, in the house of Simon the Pharisee, with an unnamed sinful woman weeping and anointing Jesus' feet.

The traditional Catholic identification — going back to Gregory the Great in the sixth century — collapsed all four stories into one and identified the woman as Mary Magdalene. That conflation is what the SAB answer about Mary Magdalene is referencing. It's textually indefensible. There's nothing in any of the four passages connecting the anointing woman to Mary Magdalene, and Luke 8:2 introduces Mary Magdalene fresh in the next chapter as if she hadn't just appeared.

The apologetic move is to argue that Luke 7 and John 12 are two separate events that just happen to share the hair-and-feet detail, while Mark/Matthew describe a third. Craig Blomberg makes this case. That's possible but strained — having a woman do the exact same unusual act of wiping Jesus' feet with her hair on two separate occasions, with two different ointments, and one of them being the same Mary of Bethany, strains plausibility.

The critical-scholarly position, articulated by Raymond Brown and developed by Fitzmyer, is that Luke and John are drawing on a common tradition of an anointing story that each evangelist has reworked. Luke moved it earlier and made it about a sinful woman to fit his Sondergut theme of Jesus and sinners. John relocated the head-anointing of Mark/Matthew to the feet and identified the woman as Mary of Bethany to tie it to the Lazarus narrative. The contradiction is the residue of multiple traditions about a memorable scene that didn't survive transmission with consistent identification.

entries.question: Did the Samaritans receive Jesus?
entries.summary: Luke 9:52-53 says a Samaritan village refused to receive Jesus because his face was set toward Jerusalem. John 4:39-40 says many Samaritans in the city of Sychar believed in him and asked him to stay, and he stayed two days. The Lukan and Johannine portraits of Samaritan response to Jesus directly contradict each other.
entries.commentary:
Luke 9:52-53 and John 4:39-40 are describing different specific incidents, so a flat contradiction reading needs to be careful. Luke's text says "a village of the Samaritans" — singular, one specific place — refused him. John says Sychar — a different specific place — welcomed him. So in a strict reading, two different Samaritan villages had two different responses. That's the obvious apologetic harmonization, and it's not stupid.

The deeper problem is that these aren't isolated narrative facts — they're stand-ins for broader theological characterizations of Samaritans in Luke and John. Luke's Gospel is famously the gospel that rehabilitates Samaritans — the Good Samaritan parable (Luke 10:25-37), the grateful Samaritan leper (Luke 17:11-19) — but Luke 9:52-53 starts the journey to Jerusalem with Samaritan rejection. John 4 is even more emphatically pro-Samaritan: Jesus has an extended theological dialogue with a Samaritan woman, declares himself Messiah to her, and the Samaritans of Sychar declare him "the Saviour of the world" in John 4:42. The two gospels are working different angles on the Samaritan question.

The historical Samaritans, as Mark Smith and Reinhard Pummer document, had real religious tensions with Jewish pilgrims passing through Samaria on the way to Jerusalem — they didn't accept the Jerusalem temple's centrality and considered Mount Gerizim the true holy mountain. So Luke 9:52-53's depiction of a village refusing a Jerusalem-bound traveler reflects plausible historical hostility. But John 4 isn't drawing on the same hostility-tradition; it's drawing on a Johannine tradition where Jesus' mission crosses ethnic and religious boundaries.

The contradiction at the literal level of "did the Samaritans receive Jesus" can be papered over by saying "some did, some didn't." The contradiction at the level of how each gospel frames Samaritan response is real and reflects different community memories, different theological agendas, and probably different historical roots in the Samaritan mission of early Christianity that Acts 8 also references.

entries.question: Was Mary blessed?
entries.summary: Luke 1:28 has Gabriel greet Mary as "blessed... among women," and Luke 1:42 has Elisabeth repeat the blessing. Luke 11:27-28 has a woman pronounce blessed the womb that bore Jesus, and Jesus replies, "Yea rather, blessed are they that hear the word of God, and keep it," redirecting the blessing away from his mother specifically.
entries.commentary:
This is a softer contradiction than most because Jesus' "yea rather" — Greek menounge — doesn't flatly deny Mary's blessedness so much as redirect it. The harmonization is actually credible here: Jesus isn't saying Mary isn't blessed; he's saying that biological motherhood isn't what makes anyone blessed, hearing-and-keeping the word is. Luke himself almost certainly didn't see a contradiction, since he wrote both passages.

That said, there's a real tension in how Luke treats the relationship between Jesus and his family. Luke 8:19-21 has Jesus' mother and brothers come to see him and Jesus says, "My mother and my brethren are these which hear the word of God, and do it" — a redefinition of family along non-biological lines. Mark 3:31-35 has an even sharper version of the same scene. The Lukan Jesus, despite the soaring infancy narratives that present Mary as a model disciple, repeatedly de-centers biological family in favor of obedience-based discipleship.

The Catholic and Eastern Orthodox traditions have done extensive work harmonizing this — Mary is the supreme example of hearing and keeping the word, so she's blessed on both counts. That's a theologically coherent move and it's textually defensible from Luke 1:38 and Luke 1:45. But Jesus' actual words in Luke 11:28 explicitly shift the basis of blessing away from "the womb that bare thee" — biological maternity — toward something anyone can do. The shift is real even if the contradiction isn't absolute.

The critical-scholarly read, going back to Brown's Mary in the New Testament collaborative volume, is that Luke is preserving two strata: an infancy-narrative tradition that celebrates Mary's unique role, and a sayings tradition shared with Mark that subordinates biological kinship to spiritual kinship. Luke harmonizes them by making Mary the exemplar of both, but the seams show.

entries.question: Who are wiser, the children of this world or the children of light?
entries.summary: Luke 16:8 has Jesus declare, in the parable of the unjust steward, that "the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light." James 3:15-17 contrasts earthly, sensual, devilish wisdom with the wisdom from above, valorizing the wisdom of those aligned with God. The Lukan saying gives the wisdom-edge to worldly people; James gives it to the heavenly-minded.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction depends almost entirely on flattening context, and the apologetic harmonization here is unusually strong. Luke 16:8 is a parable. Jesus is praising the unjust steward's shrewdness as a model for the disciples — not saying that worldly people are categorically wiser, but that they're wiser in pursuing their worldly goals than disciples often are in pursuing kingdom goals. The point is rhetorical: if scoundrels work this hard for money, why don't you work this hard for the kingdom?

James 3:15-17 isn't making a competing claim about which group is shrewder at strategic action. James is distinguishing two types of wisdom — earthly wisdom characterized by envy and strife, heavenly wisdom characterized by purity and peaceableness — and saying the latter is genuinely wise while the former just looks wise. They're not contradicting; they're using "wisdom" in different senses.

Fitzmyer's Anchor Bible treatment of Luke 16:1-13 makes the rhetorical-not-categorical reading explicit: Jesus' "wiser" in 16:8 is phronimōteroi in the Greek (comparative of phronimos) — practically shrewder, not morally wiser. The Lukan Jesus isn't ranking groups by ultimate wisdom; he's noting an asymmetry of effort. James, working in a Hellenistic-Jewish wisdom tradition closer to Sirach and the Wisdom of Solomon, is making a much more standard wisdom-versus-folly distinction.

That said, the SAB framing has a point at the populist level: someone reading the King James and stopping at the surface would see Luke saying worldly people are wiser, James saying spiritual people are wiser, and call it a contradiction. The deeper exegetical answer is that the two passages are operating on different axes — practical shrewdness versus moral-spiritual wisdom — and don't actually contradict. This is one of the weaker contradictions in the SAB list. It survives as a contradiction only on a flat, decontextualized reading.

entries.question: When was the blind man (or men) healed?
entries.summary: Matthew 20:29-30 and Mark 10:46 say Jesus healed blind men as he was departing Jericho. Luke 18:35 says Jesus healed a blind man as he approached Jericho. Matthew has two blind men, Mark and Luke have one. The three Synoptic gospels disagree on both the number of those healed and the geographic timing of the miracle.
entries.commentary:
This is a textbook Synoptic Problem case. Mark 10:46 has one blind man, Bartimaeus son of Timaeus, healed as Jesus leaves Jericho. Matthew 20:29-30 keeps the post-Jericho timing but turns one blind man into two and drops the name. Luke 18:35 keeps a single anonymous blind man but moves the healing to before Jericho — "as he was come nigh unto Jericho."

The standard apologetic harmonization runs along two tracks. Gleason Archer argues that there were actually three blind men — one Jesus encountered approaching Jericho (Luke), and two more on the way out (Matthew/Mark) — and the gospels each report partial overlapping incidents. Craig Blomberg offers a variant where Luke is describing Jesus entering the new Roman Jericho while Matthew and Mark describe him leaving the old Jewish Jericho a mile away. Both are clever and both are ad-hoc.

The Synoptic Problem solution from Joel Marcus, Ulrich Luz, and the broader two-source-hypothesis consensus is much simpler. Mark wrote first with one named blind man at the exit from Jericho. Matthew, working from Mark, doubled the figure — Matthew has a recurring pattern of doubling Mark's figures (compare Matthew 8:28's two demoniacs against Mark 5:2's one). Luke, also working from Mark, kept the single blind man but relocated the scene from the exit to the entrance because Luke 19:1-10 immediately follows with the Zacchaeus story inside Jericho — Luke needed Jesus to enter Jericho after the healing, so he moved the healing to before the entrance.

Luz's Hermeneia commentary on Matthew documents the doubling pattern, and Marcus's Mark commentary lays out the priority of Mark's account. The harmonizations require either an implausible three-blind-men coincidence or a geographic shell game involving twin Jerichos. The redactional explanation is dramatically more parsimonious: each evangelist adjusted the Markan scene for their own narrative purposes.

entries.question: Did Jesus go to heaven after he died but before his ascension?
entries.summary: Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the criminal on the cross, "To day shalt thou be with me in paradise." John 20:17 has the resurrected Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." The Lukan promise puts Jesus in paradise the day of his death; the Johannine statement keeps him from ascending until after the resurrection.
entries.commentary:
This is a clean contradiction at the surface, and the harmonizations require theological footwork. Luke 23:43 has Jesus and the repentant criminal in paradise on the day of the crucifixion — Friday. John 20:17, set on Easter Sunday or shortly after, has Jesus telling Mary not to touch him because he hasn't yet ascended to the Father.

The most common harmonization, developed across the patristic tradition and adopted by modern apologists like Norman Geisler, is that "paradise" and "the Father" are different locations. Paradise in this scheme is an intermediate state — sometimes identified with the "Abraham's bosom" of Luke 16:22, sometimes with the "prison" Christ preaches to in 1 Peter 3:19 — distinct from the heavenly throne room of the Father. Jesus could be in paradise Friday and still not have ascended to the Father by Sunday morning. That harmonization has internal logic but it's reading a complex eschatological geography into texts that don't develop one.

Another apologetic move, going back to the Greek punctuation problem, repositions the comma in Luke 23:43: "Verily I say unto thee today, shalt thou be with me in paradise." That reading saves Jesus from being in paradise Friday by making "today" modify the speech-act rather than the destination. The problem is that this is a violation of Luke's standard phrasing — Luke uses "verily I say unto thee" or "verily I say unto you" 27 times without ever pairing it with a redundant "today." The repositioned-comma reading is grammatically possible but stylistically alien to Luke.

Fitzmyer takes Luke 23:43 at its surface meaning: Jesus tells the criminal he will be with him in paradise that very day. Brown's treatment in the Death of the Messiah agrees. The most economical reading is that Luke and John have different and incompatible post-mortem itineraries for Jesus — Luke's is paradise-then-resurrection-then-ascension, John's is somewhere-not-the-Father-yet until after the resurrection. The harmonizations need to import categories not in the texts.

entries.question: When did Satan enter Judas?
entries.summary: Luke 22:3 places Satan's entering Judas before the Passover, before the Last Supper. John 13:27 places it during the Last Supper itself, immediately after Jesus hands Judas the morsel of bread. The two gospels put the satanic possession on opposite sides of the meal.
entries.commentary:
Luke 22:3-7 makes the chronology explicit: Satan enters Judas, then Judas goes to the chief priests to negotiate the betrayal, then the day of unleavened bread arrives, then the Passover meal is prepared. So in Luke, the satanic entry happens days before the Last Supper. John 13:27 is unambiguous in the other direction: at the Last Supper, after Jesus passes the sop to Judas, "Satan entered into him," and Judas immediately leaves to do the betrayal. Same event, two different times.

The standard apologetic harmonization is that Satan entered Judas twice — once initially to plant the betrayal idea (Luke 22:3), and a second time at the Supper to seal the act (John 13:27). Gleason Archer makes this move. The problem is that it's an ad-hoc duplication that neither text supports. Luke doesn't say "Satan first entered Judas"; John doesn't say "Satan again entered Judas." Both texts present the entry as a singular, definitive event.

The critical-scholarly reading, in Brown's Death of the Messiah and Fitzmyer's Anchor commentary on Luke, is that Luke and John independently developed satanic-possession traditions to explain Judas's betrayal — early Christianity had a theological problem of how a chosen disciple could betray Jesus, and demonic possession was one explanatory move. Luke front-loads the possession to make Judas's entire trajectory toward the betrayal demonically driven. John retrojects it into the Supper itself, where it produces the dramatic moment of Judas leaving into the night (John 13:30).

Both evangelists are working with the same theological tool — "the devil made him do it" — but they deploy it at different narrative moments because they're constructing different theological narratives. Luke wants the betrayal to be cosmically predetermined from the start; John wants the Supper to be the moment of cosmic confrontation. The harmonization that there were two distinct satanic entries is the textbook apologist playbook move of multiplying events to dissolve a contradiction.

entries.question: Can thieves go to heaven?
entries.summary: Luke 23:32-43 has Jesus promise paradise to the repentant thief crucified beside him. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 has Paul list thieves among those who shall not inherit the kingdom of God. Luke shows a thief admitted to heaven; Paul says thieves are excluded.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction collapses under exegetical pressure pretty quickly, but it's worth working through why. Luke 23:42-43 has the repentant criminal — Greek kakourgos, literally "evildoer," not specifically a thief — confess Jesus' lordship and Jesus promise him paradise. 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 has Paul list categories of unrighteous people who won't inherit the kingdom, then in 6:11 says "and such were some of you: but ye are washed, but ye are sanctified, but ye are justified."

The key move is 1 Corinthians 6:11. Paul isn't saying former thieves can't be saved; he's saying that ongoing unrepentant identification with these categories excludes someone from the kingdom. The Corinthian believers were thieves and fornicators and idolaters before they were washed. The kakourgos at the cross in Luke 23 confessed and was washed in the same moment — Lukan repentance is paradigmatic, and the criminal becomes a model of last-minute salvation.

So the harmonization here works: Paul and Luke aren't disagreeing on whether a repentant thief can be saved. They're addressing different questions. Luke is showing what salvation through repentance looks like at the cross. Paul is warning Corinthians against returning to or normalizing unrighteous behavior.

That said, there's a residual tension worth flagging. Paul's list in 1 Corinthians 6:9-10 reads like a categorical exclusion before 6:11 walks it back. A SAB reader pulling 6:9-10 in isolation has a reasonable case that thieves are excluded full stop. The exclusion is real at the verse level; the rehabilitation is in the next verse. This is a contradiction created by atomized prooftexting — pulling verses out of their immediate Pauline context. The contradiction is genuine on the surface but dissolves with even one additional verse of context. It's one of the weaker entries in the SAB list, and the critical-scholarly literature mostly doesn't treat this as a real tension because the verses are so close together that they belong to the same argument.

entries.question: Did Jesus drink on the cross?
entries.summary: John 19:29-30 has Jesus receive the vinegar from the sponge and then declare "It is finished." Mark 15:23 has Jesus refuse the wine mingled with myrrh. Matthew 27:34 has Jesus taste the vinegar mingled with gall and refuse to drink. The Synoptic Jesus refuses the offered drink; the Johannine Jesus drinks it.
entries.commentary:
This contradiction is partly resolvable by distinguishing two separate drink-offers in the crucifixion sequence, but only partly. Mark 15:23 and Matthew 27:34 describe an offer of drugged wine before crucifixion — Mark calls it wine mingled with myrrh, Matthew shifts the substance to vinegar mingled with gall (apparently echoing Psalm 69:21). This pre-crucifixion offer was likely a Jewish custom of providing an analgesic to the condemned, and Jesus refuses to dull his suffering.

Mark 15:36 and Matthew 27:48 then describe a second, later offer near the moment of death — a sponge of vinegar (sour wine, oxos in Greek, the cheap wine of Roman soldiers) lifted to Jesus' lips. Mark and Matthew don't specify whether Jesus drank this second offering. John 19:28-30 jumps directly to this second offer and has Jesus actively receive the vinegar.

So the partial harmonization works: there are two distinct offers, and the Synoptic refusal applies to the first while the Johannine acceptance applies to the second. Carson, Morris, and Blomberg all make this move and it holds up textually.

Where the harmonization gets thin is the question of whether Jesus drinks the second offering in the Synoptics. Mark and Matthew don't explicitly say. John says yes. So strictly speaking, only John makes a positive claim about Jesus drinking. The Synoptics neither confirm nor deny the second drink. The contradiction at the SAB level — "did Jesus drink on the cross" — yields a Synoptic "no" only if you fold the first offer (clearly refused) into the question, and ignore that the second offer is silent in the Synoptics on whether he drank.

The more interesting critical-scholarly point, in Brown's Death of the Messiah, is that John has reshaped the vinegar scene to fulfill Psalm 69:21 explicitly — "in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink" — by adding the hyssop branch and the "I thirst" cry, neither of which appears in the Synoptics. John's account is theologically elaborated. The contradiction is real if you read the question as "did Jesus consume the drink offered to him," with the Synoptic answer being ambiguous to negative and the Johannine answer being affirmative.

entries.question: Where did Jesus go when he died?
entries.summary: Luke 23:43 has Jesus promise the repentant criminal that they will be together in paradise that very day, implying Jesus went to paradise. The Apostles' Creed has Jesus descend into hell, a tradition grounded in 1 Peter 3:18-20 and 1 Peter 4:6. The biblical and creedal traditions point in opposite directions on where Jesus went between Friday and Sunday.
entries.commentary:
This is contradiction id=510 viewed from a different angle, with the added wrinkle that the "hell" answer leads with the Apostles' Creed rather than scripture. The Apostles' Creed is a fourth-century-or-later confessional document, not biblical text. The actual biblical basis for the descent-into-hell tradition is 1 Peter 3:18-20 ("by which also he went and preached unto the spirits in prison") and 1 Peter 4:6 ("the gospel preached also to them that are dead"), now added to this answer's references so the contradiction rests on scripture and not just the creedal summary.

With those passages added, the contradiction is real but narrower than "heaven versus hell" suggests. The Greek of 1 Peter 3:19 doesn't use the word for hell (hades or geenna) — it says "prison" (phylake), and the spirits there are usually identified, following the Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 traditions, with the disobedient angels of Genesis 6 and 1 Enoch. So Jesus going to the "prison of the spirits" is a specifically apocalyptic-Jewish geography rather than the medieval Christian hell.

Luke 23:43's paradise (paradeisos) is also a specifically apocalyptic-Jewish term — used in 2 Corinthians 12:4 and Revelation 2:7 for the heavenly garden, and in Second Temple texts like 1 Enoch 60:8 and 2 Enoch 8 for the dwelling of the righteous dead.

So at the technical level, Luke's Jesus goes to the heavenly paradise of the righteous, while 1 Peter's Jesus goes to the prison of the disobedient spirits. Both could in principle be true on a complex post-mortem itinerary — Augustine and Aquinas worked out elaborate schemes where Jesus visited multiple post-mortem locations — but the texts themselves don't develop such a scheme. They're two independent traditions about what Jesus did between his death and resurrection.

The critical-scholarly read is that 1 Peter is using a Jewish apocalyptic tradition (the descent to the Watchers) to give Jesus' death cosmic significance, while Luke is using a different apocalyptic tradition (paradise as righteous reward) to highlight individual salvation through the cross. The Apostles' Creed pulls 1 Peter into its summary and creates the "descended into hell" formulation that medieval Latin Christianity then elaborated. This contradiction is real but the SAB framing obscures more than it reveals.

entries.question: When did Jesus ascend into heaven?
entries.summary: Luke 24:51 has Jesus ascend on the day of resurrection itself, after a single day of post-resurrection appearances. Mark 16:19 has the ascension at the close of a sequence of appearances. John 20:26 has Jesus still on earth eight days after the resurrection, appearing to Thomas. Acts 13:31 has him appearing for many days before ascending. Acts 1:3 specifies forty days. The New Testament gives at least four different timelines for the ascension.
entries.commentary:
Acts 1:3 explicitly says Jesus was seen "forty days" before his ascension. Luke 24, written by the same author as Acts, narratively compresses the same period into what reads like a single day — Easter morning at the tomb, the Emmaus road, the appearance to the eleven, and the ascension all flow together in 24:1-51 with no narrative break for the forty days. The two Lukan works contradict each other.

The standard harmonization, developed in detail by F. F. Bruce, is that Luke 24:50-51 is a compressed summary that doesn't explicitly say the ascension happened on the same day as the resurrection — Luke just narrates events in sequence without time markers. The narrative gap between Luke 24:43 and 24:50 could accommodate the forty days. That's textually defensible but it requires the reader to import the Acts timeline into the Lukan narrative, which on its own surface reads as a single-day sequence.

John 20:26's eight-days-after-resurrection appearance to Thomas is a direct problem for any reading that compresses the ascension into the resurrection day. If Jesus is still appearing in his pre-ascension state eight days after Easter, the resurrection-day ascension reading collapses. Most apologists therefore prefer the Acts 1:3 forty-day timeline as the master schema and read Luke 24 as compressed narrative.

The Mark 16:19 reference is from the Longer Ending — Mark 16:9-20 — which Metzger and the critical-text consensus identify as a second-century addition not in Mark's earliest manuscripts (Sinaiticus and Vaticanus). So one of the four ascension timelines comes from a secondary text.

The critical-scholarly position, articulated by Mikeal Parsons in The Departure of Jesus in Luke-Acts, is that Luke had a problem: he wanted to end his gospel with the ascension as climactic closure (Luke 24), but he also wanted to begin Acts with the ascension as the bridge to Pentecost (Acts 1). He solved it by narrating the ascension twice, with two different timelines, because the rhetorical needs of the two volumes were different. The forty-day figure in Acts probably echoes the Jewish forty-day periods of Moses on Sinai and Elijah at Horeb — a theological number, not a historical datum. The contradiction is real and reflects Lukan compositional priorities, not historical witness.

entries.question: Were the disciples frightened or gladdened when they saw Jesus?
entries.summary: Luke 24:37 has the disciples terrified and affrighted, supposing they had seen a spirit when Jesus appeared. John 20:20 has the disciples glad when they saw the Lord. The two evangelists describe diametrically opposed emotional responses to the same kind of post-resurrection appearance.
entries.commentary:
This is one of the cleaner contradictions in the SAB list because both verses describe the same scene type — Jesus appearing to the assembled disciples on Easter evening — and they give opposite emotional reactions.

The standard apologetic harmonization is sequential: the disciples were first terrified (Luke 24:37), then Jesus calmed them, showed them his hands and feet, and then they became glad (John 20:20). The two reactions are stages of the same emotional arc. Norman Geisler runs this argument. It's textually defensible — Luke 24:41 actually says "they yet believed not for joy, and wondered," which captures the transition from fear to joy that the apologetic reading needs.

But the John 20:20 "then were the disciples glad, when they saw the LORD" reads as the immediate response to seeing him, not as a delayed response after initial terror. John doesn't narrate any fear phase. He has Jesus appear, say "Peace be unto you," show his hands and side, and the disciples respond with gladness. There's no Lukan terror in the Johannine telling.

The critical-scholarly read, in Brown's Death of the Messiah and the Anchor John commentary, is that Luke and John are drawing on different traditions of the Easter appearances with different emphases. Luke emphasizes the physicality of the resurrected Jesus — he shows hands and feet, eats fish, proves he's not a ghost — and the initial terror serves that emphasis by setting up the demonstration. John emphasizes the bestowal of peace and the missio of the disciples — Jesus appears, brings peace, breathes the Spirit, sends them out — and gladness serves that purpose.

The scenes aren't easily harmonized into a single chronological sequence because they're doing different theological work. The most parsimonious reading is that we have two different traditions of the Easter evening appearance, edited by two different evangelists for two different purposes. The fear-then-joy sequencing solution works at the level of "both could in principle be true" but doesn't explain why John would omit the terror that Luke makes central.

entries.question: Was it OK to touch the risen Jesus before his ascension?
entries.summary: John 20:17 has Jesus tell Mary Magdalene, "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." Matthew 28:9 has the women hold Jesus by the feet and worship him. Luke 24:39 has Jesus invite the disciples to handle him. John 20:26-27 has Jesus, still pre-ascension by John's chronology, invite Thomas to thrust his hand into his side. The Johannine prohibition to Mary directly contradicts the Synoptic and even later Johannine permissions.
entries.commentary:
This is an internal Johannine problem before it's a Synoptic-versus-John problem. John 20:17 has Jesus tell Mary not to touch him because he hasn't ascended. John 20:26-27, in the same chapter and apparently on the same temporal side of the ascension, has Jesus invite Thomas to thrust his hand into his side. Same Johannine narrative, opposite instructions.

The standard harmonization runs through the Greek. The verb in John 20:17 is haptou (present imperative middle of haptomai), which can mean "stop touching me" or "do not cling to me" rather than "do not touch me at all." Brown in the Anchor John commentary translates it "stop clinging to me" — Mary has already grabbed Jesus and won't let go, and he's telling her to release him so he can complete his return to the Father. On that reading, John 20:17 isn't forbidding touch in general but forbidding clinging, which is consistent with Thomas being invited to touch later.

That harmonization works for the Johannine internal tension. It still leaves the Matthew 28:9 conflict — there the women "held him by the feet and worshipped him," exactly the kind of grabbing behavior John 20:17 forbids Mary from doing. The Greek verb in Matthew 28:9 is ekratesan from krateo, "to grasp firmly" — the very behavior Mary is told not to do in John.

Matthew Henry and the older apologetic tradition tried to harmonize by sequencing — Matthew 28:9 happened after Jesus had "ascended" in some technical sense, John 20:17 happened before. That requires an unwarranted assumption of multiple ascensions or some technical distinction between "the" ascension and intermediate ascensions, neither of which the texts develop.

The critical-scholarly read in Brown and Davies-Allison is that Matthew and John are working from independent appearance traditions with different theological frames. Matthew's tradition emphasizes embodied recognition and worship; John's emphasizes spiritual recognition and mission. The grasping-the-feet of Matthew 28:9 and the touch-me-not of John 20:17 reflect different framings of the same kind of moment. The contradiction is real but softer than the SAB framing suggests, because John 20:17 is plausibly about clinging, not touch.

entries.question: Does Jesus judge people?
entries.summary: John 5:22, John 5:26-27, John 9:39, Acts 17:31, 2 Corinthians 5:10, and Revelation 19:11 say Jesus judges everyone, with the Father committing all judgment to the Son. John 8:15 and John 12:47 have Jesus himself say "I judge no man" and "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world." The Johannine Jesus both claims and denies the role of judge within the same gospel.
entries.commentary:
This is a Johannine internal contradiction more than a cross-canonical one. The same gospel that gives Jesus universal judicial authority in 5:22 and 5:27 has him denying that authority in 8:15 and 12:47. You can't dissolve this by appealing to authorial diversity — the same author wrote both.

The standard harmonization, in Carson's Pillar commentary and Keener's two-volume John, distinguishes between Jesus' first coming and his second coming. In the first coming Jesus' mission is salvific — "I came not to judge the world, but to save the world" (John 12:47). At the eschatological return Jesus exercises the judicial authority delegated by the Father (John 5:27). On this reading, Jesus judges no one *now*, but will judge everyone at the end. The two-mission framing is theologically coherent and it tracks how the early church developed the Christological doctrine of the first and second advents.

Brown in the Anchor John commentary makes a related but subtler move. The Johannine concept of judgment, krisis, is bivalent — judgment is simultaneously a separation and a verdict. In John 3:18-19 and 9:39, Jesus' very presence in the world functions as krisis whether or not Jesus actively pronounces verdicts — his light reveals what people are. So Jesus "judges no man" in the sense of not actively pronouncing condemnation, while simultaneously functioning as the locus of judgment by his presence. Brown calls this realized judgment.

That's elegant exegesis, but it does require the reader to hold two senses of "judge" in tension and recognize that John uses krino across both. The flat surface contradiction — "Jesus judges everyone" versus "Jesus judges no one" — is real at the verse level. The harmonization works, but it requires importing a doctrine of realized eschatology and a careful disambiguation of Greek krisis. The SAB reader pulling John 5:22 against John 12:47 isn't wrong that the words contradict; the resolution is in the conceptual framework, not the surface text.

entries.question: Did Jesus bears witness of himself?
entries.summary: John 5:31 has Jesus say, "If I bear witness of myself, my witness is not true." John 8:14 and 8:18 have Jesus say, "Though I bear record of myself, yet my record is true" and "I am one that bear witness of myself." Within the same gospel, three chapters apart, the Johannine Jesus both denies and affirms that his self-witness is valid.
entries.commentary:
This is a near-identical pair of statements making opposite claims, separated by three chapters in the same gospel. The flat-surface contradiction is stark. Note also the question text has a grammatical issue — "Did Jesus bears witness of himself?" — that should be "bear" in the underlying database.

The standard harmonization, going back to the patristic commentators and developed by Carson and Keener, reads John 5:31 as a rhetorical concession to Jewish legal standards. Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two or three witnesses for a valid testimony. Jesus in John 5:31 is acknowledging that *by that standard alone* his self-testimony wouldn't count, and then immediately marshaling additional witnesses — John the Baptist (5:33), his works (5:36), and the Father (5:37). So 5:31 is hypothetical, not a flat denial.

Then in John 8:14, Jesus shifts the argumentative frame. The Pharisees in 8:13 are appealing to the Deuteronomy 19:15 two-witness rule to dismiss Jesus' testimony, and Jesus responds that his witness *is* valid because he knows his origin and destination — he has unique epistemic access that ordinary human testimony doesn't have. In 8:18 he then adds the Father as the second witness, satisfying the legal standard.

So the harmonization runs: 5:31 concedes the two-witness rule as a baseline; 8:14 challenges the rule by appealing to Jesus' unique status; both passages then invoke the Father as the corroborating witness. That's coherent exegesis and it's how Brown reads it in the Anchor commentary.

The critical-scholarly view is that John's Jesus is constructed as a forensic figure who can both submit to and transcend Jewish legal categories depending on rhetorical context — Jesus is on trial in John, and the trial motif organizes the whole gospel. The contradiction between 5:31 and 8:14 is real at the surface level but functions as a deliberate rhetorical move in John's trial-narrative structure. The Johannine Jesus tests legal frameworks, doesn't simply submit to them. The contradiction is genuine on the surface and the harmonization requires recognizing John's literary technique. Most critical scholars don't treat this as a serious doctrinal problem because the rhetorical structure of John makes the apparent self-contradiction intelligible — but it remains a flat textual contradiction at the verse level.

entries.question: Was Jesus's witness of himself true?
entries.summary: John 8:14 has Jesus say his record of himself is true. John 5:31 has Jesus say that if he bears witness of himself, his witness is not true. John 8:18 has Jesus affirm that he is one who bears witness of himself. The same gospel both affirms and denies the validity of Jesus' self-witness.
entries.commentary:
This is functionally the same contradiction as id=519, with the question reframed from "did Jesus bear witness of himself" to "was Jesus' witness of himself true." The textual data is the same — John 5:31 versus John 8:14 — and the harmonization arguments are the same.

The harmonization, again following Carson, Keener, and the broader patristic-to-modern Johannine commentary tradition, reads John 5:31 as a rhetorical concession to the Deuteronomy 19:15 two-witness standard, not as a categorical denial of the truth of Jesus' self-testimony. Jesus is conceding that by ordinary legal standards a person's self-witness doesn't count, then marshaling additional witnesses — John the Baptist, his works, the Father, and scripture itself — to meet the legal standard. John 8:14 then claims Jesus' self-witness *is* true because Jesus has unique epistemic access to his own origin and destination, transcending the ordinary legal frame.

So the resolution depends on recognizing that John 5:31 operates within a hypothetical legal frame ("if I were the only witness, then...") while John 8:14 operates from Jesus' actual epistemic and ontological position ("because I know whence I came..."). That's the way Brown, Barrett, Keener, and Lincoln all read it.

Where this gets thin is that the SAB framing is doing something legitimate — pointing out that the surface text of John 5:31 says self-witness is not true, and the surface text of John 8:14 says it is. A flat literalist reading of either verse without the rhetorical frame produces a contradiction. The frame dissolves the contradiction only if you grant that John is constructing a complex forensic argument where Jesus tests and transcends Jewish legal categories.

This is also a duplicate of id=519 in the SAB database — the same textual data is being framed two different ways. From a database-curation perspective, IDs 519 and 520 should probably be consolidated, because they're functionally the same contradiction with cosmetic question-text variation. The Johannine evidence and harmonization arguments are identical.
